newsitem.title: FRANCE: French doctors reject govt ideas, extend strike.
newsitem.headline: French doctors reject govt ideas, extend strike.

text.p: Striking junior hospital doctors on Friday rejected government efforts to explain health system reform plans and called for an indefinite national stoppage.
The doctors continued to disrupt routine medical activities at teaching hospitals in at least 17 French cities in a challenge to the centre-right government's plans to brake spending on healthcare.
Emergency care at all hospitals is being guaranteed by non-strikers during the protests that began 10 days ago.
The strikers plan to hold a demonstration and a march on Sunday to express their dissatisfaction with the government's plans.

The government has made some concessions but it can ill afford to give in to the student doctors since reducing the health fund deficit is a key part of French efforts to qualify for a planned single European Union currency in 1999.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe said in a television interview on Thursday the government would make a big effort to explain its reforms to the strikers, saying it was widely misunderstood, but he refused doctors' calls for renegotiation.

In answer to charges that the government's reforms would result in rationing health care for purely financial reasons, Juppe insisted the government "had a medical view of the situation and not just an accountant's view".
Public health care spending is the leading factor in France's welfare deficit, expected to show a shortfall of about 33 billion francs ($5.8 billion) this year after 51.6 billion francs last year.

The strikers have been joined by some clinic directors and are supported by three unions representing mostly specialist doctors in private practice. But the largest general practitioners' union, MG France, opposes the strike.

The strike was sparked by plans to fine doctors who overshoot government-set limits on medical costs. The reforms would also impose compliance with enforceable medical standards, mandate continuous doctor training and make a personal health card compulsory for all patients.
The plan challenges the previously almost total freedom of French doctors to consult and prescribe as they wish.
The state health insurance plan, to which the vast majority of the population belongs, reimburses patients partially for any medicine, test or procedure prescribed.
